{{short description|American mathematician|bot=PearBOT 5}}
'''Joe Peter Buhler''' (born 1950 in [[Vancouver, Washington]]) is an American mathematician known for his contributions to [[algebraic number theory]], [[algebra]] and [[cryptography]].

== Education and career ==
Buhler received his undergraduate degree from [[Reed College]] in 1972, and his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1977 with thesis ''Icosahedral Galois Representations'' and thesis advisor [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy | id = 22872  | title=Joe Peter Buhler}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Buhler, Joe P.|title=Icosahedral Galois Representations|series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics 654|publisher=Springer Verlag|year=1978}} {{cite book|title=2006 pbk reprint|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JZV8CwAAQBAJ|isbn=9783540358183|last1=Buhler|first1=J. P|date=2006-11-15 | publisher=Springer }}</ref> Buhler was a professor at Reed College in [[Portland, Oregon]] from 1980 until his retirement in 2005.<ref>[https://www.reed.edu/catalog/archives/catalog_2005_06/people/faculty_emeritus.html Reed College, Emeriti]</ref>  From 2004 to 2017, he was director of the [[Institute_for_Defense_Analyses#Center_for_Communications_and_Computing|IDA Center for Communications Research]] in La Jolla, California.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Buhler|first1=Joe|last2=Graham|first2=Ron|last3=Hales|first3=Al|title="Maximally nontransitive dice"|journal=American Mathematical Monthly|volume=125|year=2018|issue=5|pages=387–399|doi=10.1080/00029890.2018.1427392}}
</ref>

In 1997, he introduced, with [[Zinovy Reichstein]], the concept of [[essential dimension]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Buhler, JP|author2=Reichstein, Z.|title=On the essential dimension of a finite group|journal=Compositio Mathematica|volume=106|issue=2|year=1997|pages=159–179|doi=10.1023/A:1000144403695|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Buhler is involved in a project to numerically verify the [[Kummer–Vandiver conjecture]] of [[Harry Vandiver]] and [[Ernst Eduard Kummer]] concerning the class number of [[cyclotomic field]]s. Vandiver proved it with a desk calculator up to class number 600, [[Derrick Henry Lehmer|Derrick Lehmer]] (in the late 1940s) to about 5000, and Buhler with colleagues (in 2001) to 12 million.<ref>J. P. Buhler, [[Richard Crandall]], Reijo Ernvall, Tauno Metsänkylä, M. Amin Shokrollahi ''Irregular primes and cyclotomic invariants to 12 million'', Journal of Symbolic Computation, Vol. 31, 2001, pp. 89–96 {{doi|10.1006/jsco.1999.1011}}</ref> He continues the project with David Harvey and others.<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=0912.2121|author=Buhler, J.P.|author2=Harvey, D.|title=Irregular primes up to 163 million|year=2009|class=math.NT}}</ref>

He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in 2012.
